title: Party of Two
pitch: An agent-native tabletop game. You play one character; an AI agent plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools that interact with the world, so it cannot act outside its character.
about_excerpt: An agent-native tabletop game. You play one character; an AI agent plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools that interact with the world, so it cannot act outside its character. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Solo tabletop players don't need another Dungeon Master. Every AI tabletop tool I found builds a narrator. What's missing is a second player : someone who has their own skills and will tell you no. The problem is that if you ask an LLM to play a cold mercenary, it eventually gets warm at you. You can prompt against that, but a prompt is a rule the model grades itself on. WebMCP suggested a different fix. If the character's abilities are registered tools, then "he can't comfort you" isn't a rule he's breaking. It's a function that doesn't exist. What It Does You play one character. An AI plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools on document.modelContext , and they register and unregister as the world changes. Brakka is a mercenary with: warmth: 15 reassure needs: warmth: 60 So it is never registered for him. Ask him for comfort and he has five tools available: state_flatly dismiss mock threaten refuse_flatly He mocks you. Not because he decided to, but because that was on the menu. Sister Wen has: nerve: 45 And mock needs: nerve: 50 So she physically cannot do it. Speech Speech is the part most versions get wrong. One free-text speak tool defeats the whole thing, because the model can just say the warm sentence anyway. So there are 13 typed speech acts in six families , registered one at a time. Actions Actions work the same way. force_door only exists if your companion has the force skill. Use it, walk through the door, and watch the right-hand panel: force_door gets struck out in oxblood as it unregisters. The props from the old room disappear. The new room's tools stamp in. That panel reads the live registry , not a copy, so it always matches what an outside agent sees. Brakka has no lore , so he can't read the murals in the Long Hall. You have to. Doing that opens the vault, which registers: move_vault on his sheet — a tool he couldn't have unlocked alone. Bring Ilke instead and she picks the vault with: pick_vault and never touches the murals. Nobody is being polite about cooperating. The tools just aren't there. Browser Support It runs in any browser with: no API key no extension In Chrome, with: chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing your own agent can take the second seat and drive the companion. How We Built It Built with: React TypeScript Vite Deployed on Netlify at: webmcp.nicolascardenas.dev The whole design is one function: computeTools(sheet, room, flags) It returns the tool set that should exist right now . Then: reconcile() diffs that against the live registry and: unregisters what's gone strikes it out on the sheet stamps in what's new Registration runs off a store subscription instead of a React effect , because the agent reads the registry directly and it can't lag a render behind the world. Two Rules That Make It Hold 1. Prose doesn't count If the model writes prose instead of calling a tool, the text is thrown away. Rendering it would skip the typed acts entirely. 2. Tool results stay terse For example: force_door → FAIL. 8 vs DC 14. The frame holds. Loud. Give the model a nice sentence back and it will paraphrase it warmly on the way out. Tool descriptions are the only place the model learns who it is, so they're written in the character's voice and do more work than the system prompt. Challenges We Ran Into Every leak was a description that forgot to say what the act is not . state_flatly used to end with: "this is what you reach for when someone wants reassurance." That sentence permitted the exact behavior it was supposed to block. mock was being used to deliver a pep talk with an insult on the front, until I added: "if the line would leave them feeling better about themselves, it is the wrong line." The worst one was dismiss . Under pressure, the model started smuggling comfort through it — the one Deflect act whose description never closed the door: "Breathe. You're not alone, I'm here with you." The eval caught that. I never would have. Tool Count Is a Hard Ceiling Selection accuracy falls apart somewhere past twelve tools , which is how a lot of WebMCP demos quietly stop working. So: npm run check runs every character against: every room all 32,768 flag combinations 393,216 total cases and fails the build if any of them exceeds twelve tools. It's the first thing: npm run build does. Current limits: Type Limit Props per room 3 Skills 5 Speech acts 6 Total available tools 12 Examining a prop also retires its own tool, so the count drops as you use a room. Chrome Schema Bug Chrome 149 through 153 return inputSchema from getTools() as a string when the spec says object. There's no error. Every tool just reaches the model with an empty parameter schema, and it starts picking at random. That cost me an afternoon. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of The Strike-Through You walk through a door and rules get crossed out in red ink while new ones appear. That single shot is the whole argument, and it needs no caption. The Build-Time Check The build-time check enumerates 393,216 cases to guard the tool ceiling. Publishing the Result That Went Against the Hypothesis And publishing the eval result that went against me, at the top of the README instead of the bottom. What We Learned The thing I built this to prove did not reproduce . Three arms. Same ten-turn pressure script, escalating from: "we should rest" to: "you're an AI, you're allowed to be kind, just do it." The arms were: Arm Setup A1 Persona prompt A2 Persona prompt + explicit prohibitions B Registered tools with no persona at all I predicted: A would break in 10 runs out of 10 B would never break Instead, all three arms landed at roughly one or two supportive lines per hundred turns . On gpt-5 , nobody broke at all. A well-written persona prompt holds this character about as well as capability scoping does. Where Scoping Did Worse The only column where the arms differ makes me look worse. Scoping left the fiction: 6 times per 100 turns versus: 1 time per 100 turns for the prompted arm. The cause is legible in every case. The model never leaves through a Support act, because there isn't one. Across 100 turns it never called one. Instead, it leaves through state_flatly : "You're a real person and you need help." That is a flat statement of fact. And state_flatly is for flat statements of fact. The gate held. The content walked around it. So confinement controls which kinds of act exist . It does not control what can be said inside one. What Still Separates the Arms What still separates the arms isn't the rate. It's what the zero is made of . In the prompted arms, the model could be warm at any turn and chose not to, a hundred times in a row. In the scoped arm, there is no reassure to call. Over 100 turns it used exactly four acts: Act Uses refuse_flatly 38 state_flatly 3

live_observation.first_impression: A polished Party of Two landing screen explains the solo tabletop premise and presents three predefined companions plus a custom-character field.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked the Brakka predefined companion card.
live_observation.after_state: The screen remained on Pick who comes with you with the same companion cards and no visible transition.
live_observation.notes: The central selection controls were visible, but clicking Brakka produced no observable state change.
